newsitem.title: UK: Blair vows anti-sleaze drive after UK MPs attacked.
newsitem.headline: Blair vows anti-sleaze drive after UK MPs attacked.

text.p: Prime Minister Tony Blair on Friday vowed to clean up standards in public life, increasing the embarrassment of opposition Conservatives who are under fire over sleaze charges that helped cost them the May 1 election.

The British parliament's ethics watchdog on Thursday criticised two former Conservative ministers for conduct "well below the standards expected of members of parliament" in accepting cash from a businessman for lobbying on his behalf.

The scathing report from standards commissioner Sir Gordon Downey said Tim Smith received at least 18,000 pounds ($30,330) from Mohammed Al-Fayed while Neil Hamilton got an amount which was unknown, but probably at least as great.

The report put new Conservative leader William Hague under pressure to take action againt the two men and against two more former Conservative legislators who Downey said failed to register lobbying fees in the register of MPs' interests. But Hague's scope for action was limited because none of those criticised was re-elected in the May 1 landslide that ended 18 years of Conservative rule and installed Labour in government with an unshakeable majority of 179.

And Hamilton, who lost his seat to an independent anti-sleaze candidate, former journalist Martin Bell, but still protests his innocence, caused a surprise by saying he could not be expelled from his local party because he was not a member.
Blair, turning the screw on a visit to his Sedgefield constituency in northeast England, contrasted his tough approach to problem MPs to that of the Conservatives.
"I can't imagine if these were Labour party members and these allegations were proven against them, that they would be staying in the Labour party," Blair told reporters.
Blair has already used sweeping new rules outlawing anything that could hurt Labour's standing to sanction two MPs facing allegations of financial irregularities.

During the election campaign, Labour attacked former prime minister John Major for failing to take tough action against MPs accused of breaching parliamentary rules to enrich themselves. Allegations MPs were paid by lobbyists to ask questions in parliament on their behalf created an impression among voters of a party grown too used to the trappings of power. Hamilton became the focus after he refused to step down as a candidate.
On Friday Blair returned to the theme: "One of the reasons we were elected was because people believed there was a need to clean up standards in public life and we will do that.

"We will put forward a whole range of measures in relation, for example, to the conduct of MPs and...to party funding. That's important because people have a right to know that the MPs they elect are going to do their jobs in a proper way." ($1=.5935 Pound)
